title: Improve a discriminant validity analysis

brief.text: In a SYNTHETIC study, constructs A and B (four items each) are hypothesised to predict C. The authors' draft says: "Discriminant validity was established with the Fornell–Larcker criterion." Run the model and review that claim.

tasks.prompt: Read HTMT, HTMT2 and the Fornell–Larcker table. Which conclusion is correct?

options.text: HTMT(A, B) is about .97, far above .85/.90, so discriminant validity of A and B is not supported, although Fornell–Larcker narrowly passes.
options.feedback: Correct. Fornell–Larcker is known to miss such problems (Henseler et al. 2015).

options.text: Discriminant validity holds because Fornell–Larcker is satisfied.
options.feedback: Fornell–Larcker passes by a margin of .003 here and has low sensitivity; HTMT clearly flags the problem.

options.text: Only C has a discriminant validity problem.
options.feedback: HTMT values involving C are moderate (about .56); the problem is A versus B.

tasks.prompt: Which responses are methodologically sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Re-examine whether A and B are conceptually distinct and compare their item wording.
options.feedback: Correct. The first question is conceptual.

options.text: If theory allows, treat A and B as one construct and report the change.
options.feedback: Correct, as a transparent, theory-based decision.

options.text: Delete items of A and B one at a time until HTMT drops below .85.
options.feedback: Automatic deletion narrows the constructs and capitalises on chance.

options.text: Report HTMT/HTMT2 instead of relying on Fornell–Larcker alone.
options.feedback: Correct. HTMT is the more sensitive criterion.

options.text: Keep the draft as it is, since the paths to C are significant.
options.feedback: Significant paths do not establish that A and B are distinct; their high overlap also makes the paths hard to interpret.

tasks.prompt: What does the overlap of A and B mean for their paths to C?

options.text: Their structural VIF is about 3.5; their separate effects are poorly identified and each f² is small.
options.feedback: Correct. Strongly overlapping predictors share most of their explanatory power.

options.text: Nothing, because PLS is robust to collinearity.
options.feedback: Path coefficients are OLS regressions and suffer from collinearity like any regression.

options.text: Their paths must be added together to get the true effect.
options.feedback: Adding partial coefficients has no general meaning.

tasks.feedbackCorrect: Correct. A converges well; its problem is not convergent validity but its overlap with B.
tasks.feedbackWrong: Not the expected value. Read the AVE row of construct A in the reliability table.

hints: Compare the Fornell–Larcker diagonal for A with the off-diagonal entry for A and B. How large is the margin?
HTMT approximates the correlation the two constructs would have without measurement error.
Good discriminant-validity remedies start from the construct definitions, not from the item list.

solution.text: HTMT(A, B) ≈ .973 (HTMT2 ≈ .973): the two constructs are empirically almost identical. Fornell–Larcker passes only by .003 (AVE(A) = .719 versus a squared correlation of .716), illustrating its low sensitivity. A and B also overlap as predictors of C (VIF ≈ 3.5, f² ≈ .02 and .03).

Sound responses: report HTMT/HTMT2, revisit whether A and B are conceptually distinct, examine item wording, and if theory permits merge them transparently or develop more discriminating items in new data. Do not delete items automatically to pass a threshold.
